column1: What three interlocking temporal dimensions must be aligned for seamless beatmatching?
column2: Phase alignment (position of transient peaks within the beat cycle), tempo synchronization (long-term BPM stability), and grid coherence (alignment of metric hierarchies like downbeats and phrase boundaries).

column1: At a 1 BPM tempo mismatch between two tracks, how much does phase offset drift per beat, and how long until it accumulates to a full beat cycle?
column2: Approximately 16.67 milliseconds of drift per beat; after 60 beats (about one minute), the offset accumulates to a full beat cycle.

column1: How small a tempo discrepancy can trained listeners detect, and within what listening window?
column2: As small as 0.2 BPM, detectable within four to eight bars of listening (corresponding to ~3.3 ms phase drift per beat).

column1: What is frequency masking, and why is it an immutable constraint rather than a mixing-board limitation?
column2: Frequency masking occurs when the ear cannot independently resolve two competing sounds in the same frequency band at similar amplitude; it results from how pressure waves physically superimpose and how the cochlea integrates overlapping spectral energy, not from equipment limits.

column1: What is the core EQ invariant for professional DJ mixing across frequency bands?
column2: At any given moment, only one primary source may dominate each critical frequency band—e.g., only one track should own the 40–100 Hz kick drum range at a time.

column1: Which frequency range is the critical vocal intelligibility zone that tolerates no competition between tracks?
column2: Roughly 2 to 4 kHz; stacking two vocal-heavy tracks here without EQ adjustment produces an unintelligible smear.

column1: Why can high-frequency percussion (hi-hats, cymbals) tolerate more overlap between two mixed tracks than kick drums or vocals?
column2: Because of their transient nature and broader spectral spread, though excessive doubling still causes listener fatigue.

column1: What is the standard phrase length unit in DJ-oriented electronic dance music, and what are its component subdivisions?
column2: The 32-bar phrase cycle, built from doubling: 4 bars = minimal hook, 8 bars = complete idea, 16 bars = full section, 32 bars = macro-phrase with exposition/development/resolution.

column1: Why does the 32-bar phrase structure allow DJs to find mix points without analyzing waveforms?
column2: Because the start of any 32-bar phrase provides a natural, structurally aligned transition opportunity shared across tracks built on this convention.

column1: What frequency ratios characterize consonant intervals (perfect fifth, major third) that make harmonic mixing sound pleasant versus dissonant?
column2: Perfect fifths have a 3:2 frequency ratio and major thirds a 5:4 ratio, producing reinforcing periodic waveforms; dissonant intervals like tritones create beating and phase cancellation perceived as roughness.

column1: What is the core invariant of energy flow architecture in DJ set construction?
column2: Tension and release: energy must be gradually accumulated (rhythmic density, harmonic anticipation, timbral brightness) before being discharged at a peak moment that feels inevitable, not arbitrary.

column1: In the DJ feedback-loop model of 'reading the room,' what happens after a track selection is made?
column2: The DJ treats the selection as a hypothesis about crowd energy shift; the next 30–60 seconds of crowd response (movement, engagement, phone use) provides confirmation or contradiction, driving rapid iterative adjustment.
